units.title: Replicated state, disjoint data ownership and DistributedSampler invariants
outcomes: Explain what each data-parallel rank replicates and what it owns: full parameters, gradients and optimizer state are replicated, while the data shard is disjoint.
Build a disjoint sharding with `DistributedSampler`, calling `set_epoch` each epoch and stating the padding and drop policy.
Predict how a sharding bug (overlap, repeat, or miscounted padding) changes the global batch.
units.why: Every rank trains a full copy of the model on its own shard. Overlapping shards or miscounted padding silently change the global batch, so ownership must be proved before any timing or scaling claim.

next.note: Proves updates match one process on the disjoint shards built here.
Syncs the replicated grads over these shards with one explicit collective.

study.title: DistributedSampler with per-epoch set_epoch
study.locator: Lines 76 to 84: the `DataLoader` with `DistributedSampler(train_data, shuffle=True, drop_last=True)`; lines 129 to 137: the `set_epoch` call before iterating, with the shuffle comment

study.title: Data partitioning and sampling strategies
study.locator: Chapter 7 Data Parallelism: Data Partitioning and Implications of Data Sampling Strategies (pp. 229 to 231); Distributed Data Parallel (pp. 242 to 243) including the Devil in the details box on DataLoaders and multiprocessing start methods (p. 243)

focus: `DistributedDataParallel` broadcasts the `state_dict` from rank 0 at construction. It never shards data; the sampler or manual offsets own disjointness.
`DistributedSampler` deals strided shards. With `shuffle=False` over 10 items and 2 ranks, rank 0 owns `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]` and rank 1 owns `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9]`.
`set_epoch` re-seeds the shuffle each epoch. Without it every epoch repeats the same order on every rank.

With `drop_last=False`, short datasets pad by repeating head indices. Over 10 items and 3 ranks each rank holds 4 indices and ranks 1 and 2 repeat 0 and 1, so token counts must account for the repeats.
units.reproduce: On CPU with no process group, build a `TensorDataset` of 10 items and two `DistributedSampler` instances with `num_replicas=2` and `shuffle=False`. Print both index lists, assert they are disjoint and their union is 0 to 9. Then repeat with 3 replicas and `drop_last=False` and show each rank holds 4 indices with the head repeats.
traps: Assuming the DDP wrapper shards batches. The guide states it does not: the wrapper syncs grads while the sampler splits data.
Forgetting `set_epoch`, then reading correlated epochs as a data bug. Same order every epoch is the default without it.
Storing resume position in the sampler. It has no `state_dict`; the loop owns the epoch integer, and the dataset version plus worker RNG must be restored beside it.

selfTest.q: What state is replicated on each rank and what differs?
selfTest.a: Parameters, gradients and optimizer state are replicated; the data shard differs. After backward the grads are averaged, so the local optimizer steps agree.

selfTest.q: Ten items over three ranks with `drop_last=False`. How many indices per rank, and which repeat?
selfTest.a: Four per rank. Rank 0 holds `[0, 3, 6, 9]`, rank 1 holds `[1, 4, 7, 0]` and rank 2 holds `[2, 5, 8, 1]`; 0 and 1 are the head repeats.

selfTest.q: `set_epoch` is never called with `shuffle=True`. What breaks?
selfTest.a: Nothing crashes, but every epoch shuffles identically, so epochs are fully correlated and any epoch-dependent analysis is wrong.

selfTest.q: Where does sampler resume position live?
selfTest.a: In the training loop as the epoch integer, not in the sampler. Resume must also fix the dataset version and worker seeding.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: sampler disjointness and union checks, padding versus drop policy, and epoch-resume equivalence.
units.stopWhen: Your CPU script prints disjoint even and odd shards for two ranks and the padded 4-per-rank lists for three ranks, and you can state what each rank replicates and what it owns without notes.

fit.note: Lambda covers construction plus sampler and set_epoch, Deep Learning at Scale covers partitioning and sampler warnings, and the mini-project supplies the sampler tests.

units.title: Loss reduction, update equivalence and the single-process oracle
outcomes: Derive when averaged rank-local mean gradients equal the full-batch gradient, and how sum reduction changes the answer by a factor of the rank count.
Implement a single-process oracle and compare losses, gradients, parameters and optimizer state under a stated tolerance.
Explain why the CS336 test shuffles with one shared seed across ranks.
units.why: Equivalence to one process is the contract that buckets, hooks, compression and sharding must all preserve. An oracle plus a tolerance turns silent scale bugs into loud failures.

next.note: Holds this equivalence fixed while accumulating over micro-steps.
Shows how DDP preserves this contract with buckets and hooks.

study.title: DDP oracle test: one process versus two disjoint shards
study.locator: Function `_test_DistributedDataParallel`: non-parallel baseline on all 20 fixture rows, per-rank disjoint 10-row shards at `offset = rank * local_bs`, 5 SGD steps at lr 0.1 with `torch.allclose` after each step, shared shuffle seed `42 + i`

study.title: Data-parallel averaging during backward
study.locator: Data Parallelism through the first optimization (overlap gradient synchronization with backward pass): per-GPU micro-batches with gradient averaging by all-reduce before the optimizer step

study.title: Sum versus mean loss across nodes
study.locator: Note on training on M nodes with batch N: summed losses give M-times-smaller grads than the single-node batch M times N; treat mean-reduction models as equivalent at the same global batch

focus: With per-rank mean loss, averaging local grads equals the full-batch mean grad. A 2-rank CPU run on an 8-row oracle matches params with `torch.allclose` at `atol=1e-6`.
With per-rank sum loss, averaging gives the full-batch sum divided by the rank count. Sum the grads, or scale the learning rate, to match a summed oracle.

The oracle fixes init, data pool and global batch, then compares loss, grads, params and optimizer state. Exact `torch.eq` can fail near `1.8e-7` across different GEMM blockings; use `assert_close` with a stated tolerance.
One shared shuffle seed keeps shards disjoint. Rank-dependent seeds can deal overlapping rows to both ranks.
units.reproduce: Run two CPU ranks on a fixed 8-row linear-regression oracle with `MSELoss` mean reduction: rank shards of 4 rows, local backward, `all_reduce` SUM then divide by 2, one SGD step. Assert both ranks match the oracle params with `torch.allclose`. Then repeat with sum reduction and show averaging misses by the rank count unless grads are summed.
traps: Comparing a mean-reduction DP run against a sum-reduction oracle and blaming the collective for the factor-of-R gap.
Demanding bitwise equality between sharded and full GEMM paths. Rounding differs by blocking; tolerance is the contract.
Shuffling per rank with rank-dependent seeds and silently overlapping shards. The shared seed is load-bearing.

selfTest.q: Two ranks hold mean-loss grads over disjoint halves. What does their average equal?
selfTest.a: The gradient of the mean loss over the concatenated batch: \((g_0 + g_1)/2\) is the full-batch mean gradient.

selfTest.q: Same setup with sum losses. What does averaging give relative to the full-batch sum gradient?
selfTest.a: The full-batch sum gradient divided by 2. Average to match a mean oracle; sum to match a sum oracle.

selfTest.q: Why does the CS336 test use `torch.manual_seed(42 + i)` on every rank before shuffling?
selfTest.a: All ranks draw the identical permutation, so the two 10-row shards stay disjoint. Different seeds per rank could overlap rows.

selfTest.q: Gathered outputs differ at `1.8e-7` on CPU. Is the all-reduce broken?
selfTest.a: No. Full versus sharded GEMM blocking rounds differently; the Picotron CPU port records exactly this gap and passes with `assert_close`.

units.title: Global batch across workers and accumulation, and no_sync
outcomes: Derive the global batch in samples and tokens from microbatch, accumulation steps and DP degree.
Implement accumulation with `no_sync` so only the final micro-step synchronizes.
Explain the two failure modes: syncing every micro-step (correct but slow) and syncing none (stale grads).
units.why: Global batch is the fixed semantic; microbatch, accumulation and worker count are interchangeable ways to reach it. `no_sync` is what makes accumulation cheaper than repeating full syncs.

next.note: Names the collective that `no_sync` skips on non-final steps.
Measures what skipping those syncs saves.

study.title: Global batch across workers and accumulation
study.locator: Revisiting global batch size: the batch equation of microbatch, accumulation and DP degree plus the maximize-dp-then-accumulate recipe; Our journey up to now for the worked large-batch example pattern

study.title: Microbatch accumulation on one GPU
study.locator: Gradient accumulation: microbatch versus global batch before data parallelism enters

study.title: Accumulation with no_sync
study.locator: Standard Implementation versus DataDistributedParalell Implementation: `maybe_sync_grads` with `model.no_sync` on non-final steps and `nullcontext` on the final step, with forward and backward inside the context

focus: Global batch is \(\text{gbs} = \text{mbs} \times \text{grad\_acc} \times \text{dp}\) in samples, times sequence length in tokens. Example: \(\text{mbs} = 2\), \(\text{grad\_acc} = 4\), \(\text{dp} = 128\) gives 1024 samples, or 4,194,304 tokens at length 4096.
`no_sync` scopes forward plus backward on non-final micro-steps; grads accumulate locally and the first step outside the context syncs.

Under mean reduction each micro loss is scaled by one over the accumulation count before backward, so the accumulated grad equals the global mean grad. A 2-rank CPU run with two halved micro-steps matches the oracle.

The Lambda Ch2 README line that `optimizer.step()` synchronizes grads is wrong for DDP: the reducer all-reduces during backward and the step is local. During accumulation only the final backward syncs.
units.reproduce: Extend the unit-2 script: split each rank shard into two micro-batches, run forward and backward inside `no_sync` with each micro loss halved, then one averaging all-reduce and one SGD step. Assert oracle match. Then move the forward outside the context and show the saving disappears while results stay correct.
traps: Wrapping only backward in `no_sync`. The DDP docs require the forward inside too, or grads still sync.
Skipping the one-over-K loss scaling under mean reduction. Accumulated grads come out K times too large, which looks like a learning-rate bug.
Reading Lambda Ch2's `optimizer.step()` sync sentence as DDP behavior. With DDP the sync point is backward; the sentence describes no real DDP run.

selfTest.q: Microbatch 2, 4 accumulation steps, 128 workers, sequence length 4096. Global batch?
selfTest.a: 1024 samples; 4,194,304 tokens (about 4M).

selfTest.q: Why scale each micro loss by one over K for K micro-steps under mean reduction?
selfTest.a: The K micro-means sum to K times the global mean; dividing restores the oracle gradient.

selfTest.q: Forward runs outside `no_sync`, backward inside. Effect?
selfTest.a: Still correct, but DDP synchronizes on that step anyway, so the accumulation saving is lost.

selfTest.q: Where does DDP synchronize: backward or optimizer step?
selfTest.a: Backward, through bucket all-reduces on grad-ready hooks. The optimizer step is local on identical averaged grads.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: accumulation and no_sync equivalence under a fixed global batch, including the loss-scaling check.
units.stopWhen: You derive the global batch both ways without notes, and your no_sync run matches the oracle while the mis-scoped variant stays correct but syncs.

fit.note: Ultrascale covers the batch equations and the dp-first recipe, Lambda covers the no_sync pattern, and the mini-project supplies the equivalence tests.

study.locator: Tests `test_DistributedDataParallel` over `ToyModel` and `ToyModelWithTiedWeights` at world size 2 on gloo: `validate_ddp_net_equivalence` broadcast check, disjoint 10-row shards, 5 SGD steps at lr 0.1 with `torch.allclose` per step; adapters `get_ddp` plus `ddp_on_after_backward`

study.title: Naive-path trap (read, do not copy)
study.locator: Class `DataParallelNaive`: `register_backward_hook` with `register_post_accumulate_grad_hook` in `_allreduce_grads` (lines 33 to 49). Read-only trap: the hook receives the parameter, so this path averages parameters and leaves `param.grad` local.

focus: Init broadcasts params from rank 0; the CS336 check `validate_ddp_net_equivalence` all-gathers the `state_dict` and asserts `allclose` on every rank.
Each rank forwards its disjoint shard (20 rows over 2 ranks gives `offset = rank * local_bs` with 10 rows each), backprops a local mean loss, then `all_reduce` SUM plus divide by world size.
The optimizer step stays local: identical averaged grads plus identical init keep replicas in sync with no per-step broadcast.
Frozen params with `requires_grad=False` carry no grads: `no_grad_fixed_param` and the `_FC2` bias stay equal and untouched.
units.reproduce: Implement `get_ddp` and `ddp_on_after_backward` in your own repo and run `pytest tests/test_ddp.py` on CPU (world size 2, gloo) until both model variants pass all 5 steps.
traps: Copying the Picotron naive hook. `register_post_accumulate_grad_hook` receives the parameter tensor, not the grad: the shipped code all-reduces weights while grads diverge (measured `-0.0538` versus `-0.0662` on two CPU ranks).
Dividing by world size twice, or never. All-reduce SUM followed by exactly one division matches the mean oracle.
Requiring grads for frozen params. The test asserts they stay equal without sync; only `requires_grad` params enter the collective.

selfTest.q: What three operations does naive DDP need, and when?
selfTest.a: Broadcast params once at init; per step, all-reduce SUM grads plus one division; local optimizer step. No per-step broadcast.

selfTest.q: The Picotron naive hook all-reduces its argument and divides. Why do grads still diverge across ranks?
selfTest.a: Its argument is the parameter. Parameters get averaged while `param.grad` stays local on every rank.

selfTest.q: 20 examples, world size 2. Which rows does rank 1 train on?
selfTest.a: Rows 10 to 19: `offset = rank * local_bs` with `local_bs` 10.

selfTest.q: Why does the test call `ddp_on_after_backward` before the optimizer step?
selfTest.a: Async implementations wait on grad handles there. A blocking naive version implements it as a no-op.

Contrast bucketed DDP with the hand-rolled per-param loop on launch count and overlap.
units.why: Buckets in reverse order are why communication starts before backward finishes. Misreading the order makes every later overlap prediction wrong.

study.title: PyTorch DDP paper: bucketing and overlap
study.locator: arXiv:2006.15704v1, Sections 3 and 5.2: reducer design, overlap through autograd hooks and buckets, default 25MB buckets with 10 to 25MB best on ResNet50 and BERT

focus: Buckets are allocated at construction in roughly reverse `Model.parameters()` order because backward readies last-layer grads first.
The reducer fires one async all-reduce per full bucket and always launches buckets in index order on every rank; mismatched order hangs or corrupts.
After backward returns, `param.grad` already holds the averaged grad on every rank; the optimizer step is local.

The CS336 overlap build is per-parameter, not bucketed: one async all-reduce per ready grad plus an explicit finish wait. This handout has no bucketed problem; buckets come from Picotron in the next unit.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw a 4-parameter model with a cap covering 2 params: place grads into buckets per the reverse-order rule, mark which bucket all-reduces first, and state when each launches relative to backward.
traps: Assuming buckets follow forward order. They follow reverse registration; forward order delays every launch.
Assuming launches follow ready order across ranks. Index order is the safety rule; ready order can differ per rank.
Adding or removing params after construction. Hooks were registered at construction for the exact set and order.

selfTest.q: Why reverse order?
selfTest.a: Backward computes last-layer grads first, so reverse registration matches readiness and buckets fill at the earliest time.

selfTest.q: The reverse-order assumption is wrong for a model. Consequence?
selfTest.a: Later launches and less overlap. Correctness holds; speed does not.

selfTest.q: Why bucket index order instead of ready order?
selfTest.a: Every rank must invoke matching all-reduces in the same order; otherwise backward hangs or grads mismatch.

selfTest.q: CS336 overlap versus DDP buckets?
selfTest.a: CS336 launches one async all-reduce per ready param plus a finish wait; DDP groups params into buckets for fewer launches with the same overlap idea.

study.title: Bucket-size sweep
study.locator: arXiv:2006.15704v1, Section 5.2: bucket-size sweep with 10 to 25MB best on ResNet50 and BERT; extremes lose to launch overhead or late starts

study.title: Bucket and overlap trade-offs
study.locator: Chapter 4: Overlapping Communication and Computation (Pipelining), Reducing Communication Frequency and Volume, and Achieving Maximal Overlap in Practice; default 25MB buckets, large buckets use bandwidth but delay first launch, small buckets start early but add overhead

focus: Bucket count follows the cap: a 50 MiB fp32 grad set at a 25 MiB cap gives 2 buckets and 2 all-reduces per step. Total bytes stay identical; only launch count and timing change.
Picotron accumulates each ready grad into its `main_grad` bucket view, fires async all-reduce per full bucket during backward, and copies back to `param.grad` after the wait.
The paper sweep peaks in the middle (10 to 25MB): tiny buckets drown in launch overhead, giant buckets start late and barely overlap.
One giant bucket means one end-of-backward all-reduce with almost no overlap. Treat any larger-is-sooner claim as workload-specific until your timeline says otherwise.
units.reproduce: On a 4-param toy with a cap covering exactly one param versus all params, count the launches per step (4 versus 1) and show identical averaged grads; state the launch-count rule.
traps: Reading fewer launches as fewer bytes. Bytes are fixed by the parameter count and rank count; bucketing only regroups them.
Expecting overlap from a single giant bucket. With one bucket the all-reduce waits for the last grad.
Quoting CPU gloo timings as NCCL evidence. Order and equality transfer; timings do not.

selfTest.q: 50 MiB of fp32 grads, 25 MiB cap. Buckets and launches per step?
selfTest.a: 2 buckets, 2 all-reduces. Same bytes as one 50 MiB all-reduce, different timing.

selfTest.q: Why can smaller buckets hurt?
selfTest.a: Per-launch latency and overhead dominate, and fragmentation grows; the middle range wins.

selfTest.q: What does `_post_backward` do and when does it run?
selfTest.a: Queued once per backward; waits for all bucket handles, then copies `main_grad` into `param.grad` before the optimizer step.

selfTest.q: A source says raising the cap launches sooner. Right?
selfTest.a: Not in general. Larger buckets fill later; they move bytes more efficiently but start later.
